::: {#thm-conditional-odds-ratio-reversible}

#### The conditional odds ratio is reversible

Let:

- $X$ and $Y$ be [binary](data.qmd#def-binary-var) random variables, each with values $0$ and $1$.
- $Z$ be a random variable, and $z$ be a value of $Z$.
- $\Pf{X = x, Y = y, Z = z} > 0$ for each $x, y \in \set{0, 1}$.

The [odds ratio](#def-odds-ratio) of $Y = 1$ comparing $X = 1$ with the [reference group](#def-reference-group) $X = 0$, among the units with $Z = z$, equals the odds ratio of $X = 1$ comparing $Y = 1$ with $Y = 0$, among the units with $Z = z$:

$$
\orf{Y \mid X, Z = z} = \orf{X \mid Y, Z = z}.
$$

:::

::: proof
First, find the [odds](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-odds) of $Y = 1$ in the group $X = x$ among the units with $Z = z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\odds_{x}
&= \frac{\Pf{Y = 1 \mid X = x, Z = z}}{1 - \Pf{Y = 1 \mid X = x, Z = z}}
&& \text{(definition of odds)}
\\ &= \frac{\Pf{Y = 1 \mid X = x, Z = z}}{\Pf{Y = 0 \mid X = x, Z = z}}
&& \text{(the two values of $Y$ have conditional probabilities that sum to 1)}
\\ &= \frac{\Pf{X = x, Y = 1, Z = z} / \Pf{X = x, Z = z}}{\Pf{X = x, Y = 0, Z = z} / \Pf{X = x, Z = z}}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability, in numerator and denominator)}
\\ &= \frac{\Pf{X = x, Y = 1, Z = z}}{\Pf{X = x, Y = 0, Z = z}}
&& \text{(divide the numerator and the denominator by the same positive number $\Pf{X = x, Z = z}$)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The [odds ratio](#def-odds-ratio) is the odds $\odds_1$ divided by the odds $\odds_0$.
Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal, so

$$
\orf{Y \mid X, Z = z}
= \frac{\Pf{X = 1, Y = 1, Z = z} \Pf{X = 0, Y = 0, Z = z}}{\Pf{X = 1, Y = 0, Z = z} \Pf{X = 0, Y = 1, Z = z}}.
$$

The same steps with the roles of $X$ and $Y$ exchanged give

$$
\orf{X \mid Y, Z = z}
= \frac{\Pf{Y = 1, X = 1, Z = z} \Pf{Y = 0, X = 0, Z = z}}{\Pf{Y = 1, X = 0, Z = z} \Pf{Y = 0, X = 1, Z = z}}.
$$

The event $\set{Y = y, X = x, Z = z}$ is the event $\set{X = x, Y = y, Z = z}$, so each joint [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) here equals the joint probability with its arguments in the other order.
The denominator is a product of two joint probabilities, and multiplication is commutative.
Reordering its two factors gives the denominator of the first display.
:::
